procedural_history.originating_court: District and Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court No. III, Coimbatore
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 27.09.2013 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal Revision Case Nos. 1657 and 1658 of 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent-accused, aggrieved by the judgment of the District and Sessions Judge, filed Criminal Revision Nos. 1657-1658 of 2008 before the Madras High Court. The High Court, exercising its revisional jurisdiction, reversed the concurrent findings of the Courts below and set aside the judgment of conviction and sentence passed against the accused. The appellants were unrepresented during the final hearing, and the hearing proceeded ex parte.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant-complainants, aggrieved by the High Court's judgment, filed Special Leave Petitions before the Supreme Court, which were converted into Criminal Appeals Nos. 950-951 of 2018. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals.

directions: The impugned order dated 27.09.2013 passed in Criminal Revision Petition Nos. 1657 and 1658 of 2008 is hereby set aside.
The order of Conviction and Fine passed by the Trial Court is restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondent-accused successfully rebutted the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

facts: The appellants, after resigning as directors from the respondent's company, demanded repayment of capital they had infused.
The respondent issued a promissory note and two cheques in favour of the appellants to discharge this liability.
The respondent admitted to signing the cheques and the promissory note.
The respondent's defense was that the cheques were not issued for a debt, but as a form of security.
law: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments (N.I.) Act, once a cheque is signed and issued, there is a statutory presumption that it is for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
The burden of proof to rebut this presumption lies with the issuer of the cheque (the accused).
application: The Court started its analysis by noting that the respondent's admission of signing the cheques automatically triggered the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act.
This shifted the burden of proof to the respondent to show that the cheques were issued for a purpose other than discharging a debt, such as for security.
The Court found that the respondent "failed to rebut the presumption by adducing any cogent or credible evidence."

Conversely, the Court was convinced by the "over-whelming evidence" presented by the appellants which established that the cheques were, in fact, issued to discharge an existing and legally enforceable debt.
Since the respondent did not provide sufficient evidence to support his claim, his defense was rejected, and the presumption remained in force.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the respondent failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act. The Court held that because the respondent admitted to signing the cheques, the presumption that they were for a legally enforceable debt was activated, and he failed to provide any credible evidence to prove otherwise.

issue.issue_text: Whether the issuance of a cheque and a promissory note on the same date is sufficient to raise a doubt and rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act, treating the cheque merely as a security for a loan.

facts: Appellants, after resigning as directors from the respondent's company, demanded repayment of their dues.
The respondent issued a promissory note and two cheques in favour of the appellants to discharge this liability.
The respondent admitted to signing the cheques and the promissory note.

The High Court had previously accepted the respondent's argument that because the cheques and the promissory note were issued on the same date, the cheques should be treated merely as security for a loan, which raised a doubt about the existence of a legally enforceable debt.
law: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments (N.I.) Act, once a cheque is signed and issued, there is a statutory presumption that it is for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
This presumption is rebuttable, meaning the person who issued the cheque (the drawer) has the burden to prove that it was issued for a different purpose, such as a security for a loan.
application: The Supreme Court began its analysis by noting that since the respondent admitted to signing the cheques, the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act was automatically activated.
This shifted the burden of proof to the respondent to show that the cheques were not for an existing debt.

The Court found that the respondent's argument—that the simultaneous issuance of the promissory note and the cheques was enough to create doubt—was insufficient. The respondent "failed to rebut the presumption by adducing any cogent or credible evidence."
In contrast, the Court found that the appellants had provided "over-whelming evidence" establishing that the cheques were indeed issued to discharge an existing and legally enforceable debt.
Therefore, the mere fact that a promissory note was issued on the same day as the cheques was not considered sufficient evidence to rebut the strong statutory presumption.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the issuance of a cheque and a promissory note on the same date is not, by itself, sufficient to raise a doubt and rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act. The respondent failed to provide any credible evidence to support his claim that the cheque was merely for security, and thus did not discharge his burden of proof.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondent-accused successfully rebutted the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
appellant_arguments: The respondent admitted his signatures on the dishonoured cheques and the promissory note, which triggers the presumption under Section 139.
The appellants provided overwhelming evidence to prove the cheques were issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt, which arose from the respondent's failure to return their share in a company.
The respondent failed to adduce any cogent or credible evidence to rebut the statutory presumption.
respondent_arguments: The cheques were not issued towards the discharge of a legally enforceable debt.
The respondent had refuted the appellants' claim.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the issuance of a cheque and a promissory note on the same date is sufficient to raise a doubt and rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act, treating the cheque merely as a security for a loan.
appellant_arguments: The cheques were issued to discharge an existing liability and a legally enforceable debt.
The fact that the respondent signed both the cheques and a promissory note strengthens the presumption that a debt existed.
respondent_arguments: The cheques were not issued to discharge a debt but were given as a security.

cases.principle: Once the signature on the cheque is admitted, the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt would operate, and the burden shifts to the accused to rebut it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a cheque is issued in favour of a holder, there is a rebuttable statutory presumption that it is issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. The burden is on the issuer of the cheque to rebut this presumption by proving it was issued for some other purpose.
obiter: The respondent having admitted that the cheques and Pronote were signed by him, the presumption under Section 139, NI Act would operate.
The respondent failed to rebut the presumption by adducing any cogent or credible evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Once the respondent admitted to signing the cheques and the promissory note, the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act that the cheques were issued for a legally enforceable debt was triggered. The respondent subsequently failed to rebut this presumption by adducing any cogent or credible evidence, whereas the appellants had provided overwhelming evidence to prove their case.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 139 of the N.I. Act, once a cheque has been signed and issued in favour of the holder, there is statutory presumption that it is issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. This presumption is a rebuttable one, if the issuer of the cheque is able to discharge the burden that it was issued for some other purpose like security for a loan.
why_appellant_won: The appellants have proved their case by over-whelming evidence to establish that the two cheques were issued towards the discharge of an existing liability and legally enforceable debt.
The respondent having admitted that the cheques and Pronote were signed by him, the presumption under Section 139, NI Act would operate.
why_respondent_lost: In the present case, the respondent has failed to produce any credible evidence to rebut the statutory presumption.
